title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Dashwood family had lived in Sussex for a very long time. They owned a large estate and made their home at Norland Park, in the middle of their land. For many generations they had lived there with a respectability that won the general approval of everyone they knew in the neighbourhood. The estate's last owner was an unmarried man who lived to a great age. For many years his sister had kept him company and managed his household. Her death, ten years before his own, changed his home considerably. To fill the gap she left, he invited his nephew, Mr. Henry Dashwood, and his family to live with him. This nephew was the legal heir to Norland, and the person he intended to leave it to. With his nephew and niece and their children around him, the old gentleman passed his days in comfort, growing steadily more attached to them all. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Dashwood constantly attended to his wishes, out of real kindness as well as an interest in their future inheritance. They gave him every substantial comfort his age allowed, while the children's cheerfulness brought a fresh enjoyment to his life.

Mr. Henry Dashwood had a son by his first marriage and three daughters by his present wife. His son, a dependable, respectable young man, was already well provided for. His mother's fortune had been considerable, and half of it had passed to him when he came of age. A marriage of his own soon afterwards added still more to his wealth. Inheriting Norland was therefore much less important to him than it was to his sisters. Apart from whatever their father's inheritance might bring them, the girls could expect very little money. Their mother had no fortune, and their father had only seven thousand pounds that he could freely dispose of. The other half of his first wife's money was also reserved for her son; Henry had only the right to its income during his lifetime.

The old gentleman died. His will was read and, like almost every will, caused as much disappointment as satisfaction. He was neither unfair nor ungrateful enough to leave the estate away from his nephew—but the conditions he attached to the inheritance destroyed half its value. Mr. Dashwood had wanted it more for his wife and daughters than for himself or his son. Yet it was secured to his son and his son's son, a child of four, on terms that left him unable to provide for those he loved most and who most needed help. He could neither raise money against the estate nor sell its valuable timber for their benefit. Everything was tied up for the child. On occasional visits to Norland with his parents, this little boy had won his uncle's affection with attractions by no means rare in children of two or three: indistinct speech, a firm determination to get his own way, plenty of sly little tricks, and a great deal of noise. These had outweighed all the years of attention the old gentleman had received from his niece and her daughters. He had no wish to be unkind, however. As a sign of his affection for the three girls, he left each of them a thousand pounds.

At first Mr. Dashwood was bitterly disappointed. But he was naturally cheerful and hopeful, and could reasonably expect to live for many years. By keeping his expenses low, he might save a considerable amount from the income of an estate already large and capable of improvement almost at once. Yet the fortune that had taken so long to reach him remained his for only a year. He outlived his uncle by no more than twelve months, and all that was left for his widow and daughters, including the recent legacies, was ten thousand pounds.

As soon as his condition was known to be dangerous, his son was sent for. With all the strength and urgency his illness allowed, Mr. Dashwood entrusted the welfare of his son's stepmother and sisters to his care.

Mr. John Dashwood did not share the rest of the family's depth of feeling. Still, such an appeal, made at such a moment, moved him, and he promised to do everything he could to make them comfortable. The assurance put his father's mind at rest. Mr. John Dashwood then had time to consider how much, in prudence, he could actually afford to do for them.

He was not a bad-hearted young man, unless being rather cold-hearted and rather selfish amounts to being bad-hearted. In general, people respected him, since he behaved properly in carrying out his everyday duties. A kinder wife might have made him more worthy of respect still; she might even have made him kind himself. He had married very young and was extremely fond of his wife. Mrs. John Dashwood, however, was an exaggerated version of her husband, with an even narrower mind and greater selfishness.

When he made the promise to his father, he privately intended to add a thousand pounds to each of his sisters' fortunes. At that moment he genuinely believed he could afford it. The prospect of four thousand a year on top of his existing income, together with the remaining half of his mother's fortune, warmed his heart and made generosity seem possible. “Yes, he would give them three thousand pounds. It would be a generous, handsome gift! It would be enough to set their minds completely at ease. Three thousand pounds! Even so considerable a sum could be spared with very little inconvenience.” He thought about it throughout that day and for several days afterwards, without regretting his decision.

The funeral was scarcely over when Mrs. John Dashwood arrived with her child and their servants, having given her mother-in-law no warning that she intended to come. Nobody could question her right to do so: the house had belonged to her husband from the instant of his father's death. But that only made her lack of tact more glaring. Any woman in Mrs. Dashwood's position, with ordinary feelings, would have found it deeply unpleasant. Her own sense of honour was so acute, and her generosity so romantic, that an offence of this sort, whoever committed or suffered it, provoked in her a disgust that nothing could shake. Mrs. John Dashwood had never been liked by her husband's family. Until now, however, she had lacked an opportunity to show just how little she could consider other people's comfort when circumstances suited her.

Mrs. Dashwood felt this ungracious behaviour so keenly, and despised her daughter-in-law so thoroughly for it, that she would have left the house for ever the moment the other woman arrived. Her eldest daughter pleaded with her to consider first whether leaving was the proper course. Then her tender love for all three of her children persuaded her to stay, and for their sake to avoid a quarrel with their brother.

Elinor, the eldest daughter whose advice had such influence, had a strong understanding and a calm judgment. Though only nineteen, she was fitted to advise her mother. Often, to everyone's benefit, she could check the impulsive enthusiasm that would otherwise have led Mrs. Dashwood into unwise decisions. She had an excellent heart: she was affectionate by nature and felt things deeply. But she knew how to control her feelings—a lesson her mother had still to learn, and one of her sisters had decided she would never be taught.

In many ways Marianne was just as able as Elinor. She was intelligent and thoughtful, but passionate about everything; neither sorrow nor joy could ever be moderate with her. She was generous, lovable, engaging—everything, in fact, except cautious. The resemblance between her and her mother was extraordinarily strong.

Elinor watched her sister's excessive emotional sensitivity with concern; Mrs. Dashwood prized and encouraged it. Mother and daughter now urged each other on in the intensity of their grief. The anguish that had first overwhelmed them was deliberately revived, sought out, and created afresh again and again. They surrendered themselves entirely to sorrow, dwelling on every thought that could make them more miserable and resolving never to accept comfort in the future. Elinor too was deeply grieved, but she could still struggle against her suffering and make an effort. She could discuss matters with her brother, welcome her sister-in-law on her arrival and give her the attention due to her. She could also try to stir her mother to the same effort, and encourage her to show the same restraint.

Margaret, the remaining sister, was cheerful and good-natured. But she had already absorbed a good deal of Marianne's romantic thinking without much of her good sense. At thirteen, she therefore showed little promise of matching either of her sisters when she was older.
